transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-10-29 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Everbay Head of Platform), Rajiv Kapoor (Everbay Security Lead), Tom Ellis (Everbay SRE), Asha Patel (Everbay Networking)

Summary:
Quick discovery to validate Everbay's network posture and constraints for a Private/VPC onramp. Main asks: region restrictions, VPC peering vs privatelink, transit gateway interactions, KMS and audit log workflow, and pilot timeline. Action items and a follow-up hands-on workshop agreed.

Topics covered:
- Current infra and security posture
- VPC peering/topology options (direct peering, Transit Gateway, Private Endpoints / PrivateLink)
- Regional constraints & data residency
- Egress IPs, NAT, and firewall allowances
- KMS/HSM and encryption in flight/at rest
- Rollout plan (pilot -> staging -> prod) and success criteria

Action items (quick list): see metadata fields.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Lena Park: Hi everyone, thanks for making time, I'm Lena from Redwood, AE on the account. Diego my SE will run through the technical constraints. Is this time still good for Everbay?
[00:08] Maya Chen: Yep, perfect. We have about an hour, very curious to see what the onramp looks like.
[00:12] Rajiv Kapoor: Morning/afternoon all. High level: Everbay is regulated finance, so we need SOC2, audit logs, KMS integration, and strict regional residency for a handful of customers.
[00:22] Diego Ramos: Totally understood. We'll surface how Private works — VPC peering vs private endpoints, and what the network footprint looks like. Quick question: are you leaning toward a dedicated appliance or full private deployment inside your VPC?
[00:34] Maya Chen: We want private deployment (Redwood Private) ideally behind our VPC. But we'll evaluate dedicated reserved capacity as a fallback if the on-prem/hardware integration is too heavy. Primary requirement is data never leaves our VPC — or at least, goes through our controlled egress.
[00:48] Tom Ellis: We also need static egress IPs for allowlisting. We run strict firewalls and some legacy partners expect static ranges.
[00:55] Diego Ramos: Okay, we can support stable egress via NAT gateway in your account or by routing through a customer-managed egress. For Private we typically offer two patterns: 1) Private endpoints (privatelink-style) where Redwood hosts a VPC endpoint and you connect via interface endpoints, or 2) direct VPC peering / TGW where Redwood's service VPC peers to your VPC and traffic stays on the backbone. Each has tradeoffs.
[01:16] Asha Patel: Can you elaborate on TGW? We have a Transit Gateway with many spokes; we try to centralize egress through a hub.
[01:22] Diego Ramos: Sure. With TGW you can attach Redwood's VPC into the hub, or we can peer to a spoke. The considerations are BGP and route table management, plus whether you want the data plane to flow through your hub for inspection. TGW lets you centralize inspection, which many banks prefer.
[01:36] Maya Chen: Route table churn is a concern — we can't accept CIDR overlaps with internal services. Our infra team will provide the CIDR blocks but we want minimal manual changes.
[01:45] Lena Park: From a rollout perspective, many customers start with private endpoints because it's less invasive — we stand up endpoints in the Redwood-managed account and you create interface endpoints in your VPC. But if you require TGW-level inspection or a fixed egress IP, peering + NAT in your account is common.
[02:04] Rajiv Kapoor: How does KMS work? We use a customer-managed KMS key in AWS for at-rest encryption. We can't hand over keys.
[02:10] Diego Ramos: You can use your CMK (customer-managed key). Redwood Private supports integrating with your KMS via IAM roles and we never store plaintext keys. We'll provide docs for the required IAM policy. A few customers also push keys into an HSM — we can work through the HSM/KMS integration.
[02:26] Tom Ellis: Audit logs — we need push of request and response hashes to our SIEM. Is log forwarding available?
[02:31] Lena Park: Yes, audit logs are configurable. For Private we can send structured logs to your S3 or push to your EventBridge/Kinesis. We also offer token-level tracing in Redwood Console.
[02:42] Maya Chen: There's also region gating — we operate in eu-west-1 and us-east-1 primarily. Some clients require EU-only processing. Can Redwood guarantee processing in eu-west-1 for EU customers?
[02:53] Diego Ramos: For Private deployments we can ensure the inference nodes are in your specified region. Our control plane may be region-aware; if you need full control plane isolation we offer Private with a customer-managed control plane option. For hosted models region constraints are trickier, but Private solves that.
[03:10] Rajiv Kapoor: Any implications for latency when using interface endpoints vs peering?
[03:15] Diego Ramos: Peering usually has slightly lower latency since it's intra-cloud backbone without the extra ENI hops. Interface endpoints add a small ENI hop and could increase p95 by a few ms. For most applications it's negligible, but for ultra-low latency trading use-cases we'd recommend peering and co-located region nodes.
[03:32] Maya Chen: We also have compliance that forbids cross-account storage of PII. How does Redwood handle cached prefixes or KV caches?
[03:40] Diego Ramos: By default Redwood can configure zero-persistent-cache for your tenant and disable prefix caching. If you need, we can enforce KV cache eviction and keep all ephemeral caches in your VPC.
[03:49] Tom Ellis: On certificates and mTLS — do you support mutual TLS for the data plane?
[03:54] Lena Park: Yes, mTLS is supported when using private endpoints. We'll share the cert signing and rotation process; many customers rotate on a 90-day schedule.
[04:04] Asha Patel: What's the expected network ACL and security group configuration we need to apply on our side?
[04:10] Diego Ramos: For interface endpoints, open outbound to the Redwood endpoint ENIs on the required ports (HTTPS), and optional whitelisting of Redwood's peering CIDRs if you go that route. We'll provide a playbook and CloudFormation/Terraform snippets.
[04:27] Maya Chen: Sounds good. On billing — if we do Private behind our VPC do we pay token usage as hosted or is there a flat infra fee?
[04:35] Lena Park: Private has a platform fee plus usage. For Dedicated reserved capacity there's an annual/quarterly commit option that reduces per-token cost. We'll prepare a high-level pricing sheet for Private vs Dedicated (attached in follow-up).
[04:49] Rajiv Kapoor: Any known conflicts with our security vendors — we use a third-party WAF and a packet capture appliance in the TGW.
[04:56] Diego Ramos: Those are common. For packet capture we recommend mirroring from your spoke or hub; Redwood doesn't require access to the packet capture. For WAFs, the inspection point matters — place WAF in front of the Redwood traffic if you need HTTP-layer inspection.
[05:11] Tom Ellis: Is there any onboarding window where we need to open CIDRs to Redwood team accounts for provisioning?
[05:16] Lena Park: Minimal. During provisioning we might request temporary connectivity for bootstrap, but long-term we rely on your interface endpoints or peering you control.
[05:24] Maya Chen: Okay, let's get into specifics. I'll hand over to Asha and Tom for networking and Rajiv for security specifics.
[05:31] Asha Patel: We have overlapping RFC1918 ranges in some legacy VPCs. Our preferred pattern is to attach Redwood to our TGW hub and use route filters — we cannot renumber subnets for a pilot. Can Redwood accept asymmetric routing where return traffic goes via the hub?
[05:45] Diego Ramos: We can support asymmetric routing if you handle the NATing and maintain consistent SNAT answers; we just need to ensure session stickiness for the inference traffic. For best results we recommend a small, dedicated CIDR for the Redwood endpoints to avoid overlaps.
[05:58] Rajiv Kapoor: Also, we have a policy that keys must never be exported. How will Redwood request KMS permissions?
[06:04] Diego Ramos: We ask for decrypt/encrypt permissions for the CMK via an IAM role in your account. We never transfer the private key material. The policy is scoped to the Redwood service principals and can be audited.
[06:16] Lena Park: Quick process note: typical flow is discovery -> networking workshop -> pilot environment (2-4 weeks) -> ramp. Any blockers early are typically CIDR collisions and compliance paperwork.
[06:27] Maya Chen: Timeline-wise, we want a pilot before end of Q4. Is that realistic?
[06:31] Lena Park: Yes, that's realistic if we get the artifacts this week — CIDRs, TGW attachments, and a compliance POC contact.
[06:38] Tom Ellis: For the pilot, do we need dedicated GPU capacity or can we use a smaller shared fleet? Latency sensitivity varies by model and route.
[06:47] Diego Ramos: We can start on a small dedicated pool for your tenant in your region, or even a co-tenanted private instance with isolations. We'll propose a couple of sizing options after we learn your token volume and p95 targets.
[06:59] Rajiv Kapoor: Any encryption of data in motion beyond TLS? Forward secrecy?
[07:03] Diego Ramos: We use TLS 1.3 with forward secrecy. For Private we can also enable mTLS as mentioned.
[07:09] Maya Chen: On the region gating, if we have EU-only customers, can we route EU traffic to eu-west-1 and US traffic to us-east-1 with the same model version?
[07:17] Diego Ramos: Yes, with multi-region deployment of the model. You'll pin model versions per region. Our runtime supports consistent model versions across regions; there will be replication of model artifacts.
[07:29] Lena Park: At this point I want to capture next steps: Diego will draft three topology options, we'll send SOC2 + KMS docs, and Everbay will share CIDR/TGW details.
[07:40] Maya Chen: We'll share that by Monday. Also would like a short checklist for firewall rules to hand to infra.
[07:47] Lena Park: We'll include a Terraform snippet.
[07:50] Asha Patel: One more question — how do you handle fallback if private capacity hits limits? E.g., do you fail open to hosted?
[07:58] Diego Ramos: Good question. By default Private will fail closed, but we can configure fallback policies — route to a dedicated Redwood pool in the same region or notify and hold requests. Fallbacking to hosted will require contractual agreement because of data residency.
[08:15] Rajiv Kapoor: Ok can't do hosted fallback for EU PII.
[08:19] Lena Park: Noted. We'll document fallback policies and a hard-stop for EU-marked traffic.
[08:26] Tom Ellis: Are there performance benchmarks we can run? We want p50/p95 for a 2K token sequence.
[08:33] Diego Ramos: Yes, we'll run a short benchmark in the pilot with your prompt set. We'll provide the harness and results.
[08:39] Maya Chen: Great. Anything else from Redwood?
[08:42] Diego Ramos: I'll also call out egress bandwidth — for high QPS you may want to provision additional TGW bandwidth or peering. We'll show network throughput numbers in the options doc.
[08:53] Lena Park: I'll consolidate and send the security pack plus the pricing note.
[08:58] Maya Chen: Perfect. Let's end with a quick recap and owners.
[09:02] Lena Park: Recap: Diego -> VPC topology options & diagram; Lena -> SOC2/KMS docs + pricing; Everbay -> CIDRs, TGW details, egress constraints. Schedule workshop for early next week.
[09:16] Maya Chen: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[09:19] Rajiv Kapoor: Thanks, bye.
[09:21] Tom Ellis: Bye.
